title: Demand-pull and cost-push inflation

match.reason: The closest bank point, e-inflation, covers both demand-pull and cost-push causes, but it is broader because it also teaches the effects of inflation on consumers, savers, firms and government, so it does not match this point exactly.

draft.title: Demand-pull and cost-push inflation
card: inflation caused by total spending (aggregate demand) growing faster than the economy's capacity to produce. Firms cannot supply enough, so buyers compete and prices rise.
inflation caused by a rise in the costs of production, such as wages, energy or imported materials. Firms pass the higher costs on by raising prices.
Demand-pull shows up as a rise in aggregate demand. Cost-push shows up as a fall in aggregate supply, so the economy produces less at each price level.
To tell them apart, ask what started the price rise: more spending pressing on limited capacity, or higher costs of making goods and services.
draft.remember: Demand-pull starts with spending. Cost-push starts with the costs of production.

a.q: Which situation is an example of demand-pull inflation?
opts: Household spending surges and firms cannot produce enough
A drought raises the cost of growing wheat for bakers
A fall in the dollar makes imported parts dearer for firms
A rise in power prices lifts the costs of factories
a.why: Spending growing faster than capacity is the cause of demand-pull inflation. The other three start with higher costs of production, so they are cost-push. A price rise alone does not tell you the type, the starting cause does.
a.clue: Look for the option where the push comes from buyers, not from costs.

b.q: Mia runs a bakery in Ballarat. Flour and electricity both become dearer, so she lifts her bread prices, though customer numbers have not changed. What type of inflation is this, and why?
opts: Cost-push, because her costs of production rose
Cost-push, because her customers now spend less
Demand-pull, because her costs of production rose
b.why: Her costs rose first, and she passed them on. Customer numbers did not change, so spending did not start the rise. That makes it cost-push. Demand-pull needs spending to grow faster than capacity, and a price rise by itself does not show that.
b.clue: Ask what changed first: spending or costs?

a.best: Household spending surges and firms cannot produce enough

b.best: Cost-push, because her costs of production rose
